quote: Theorem 1. If F ∈ H, then F satisfies (SD).
family: inverted concave class H: F(1/x) concave in x ∈ R++ (equivalently, for densities, x²f(x) increasing); includes infinite-mean Pareto, Fréchet (α ≤ 1), absolute Cauchy, inverse Gamma (α ≤ 1), Feller–Pareto (γ ≥ γ1), etc.
compared: linear combinations ΣηiXi vs ΣθiXi of iid X ~ F under majorization of weights

hypotheses.formal: the (SD) relation itself: ΣηiXi ≤st ΣθiXi for θ ≼ η

hypotheses.text: X1, ..., Xn iid with infinite mean (implied by (SD))

conclusion.direction: ΣηiXi <=st ΣθiXi whenever θ ≼ η (more equal weights give stochastically larger combination)

quantifiers: all θ, η ∈ Rn+, n >= 2, all x

quote: Proposition 3. Let X1, . . . , Xn ∼ F be iid where F ∈ H. For vectors (θ1, . . . , θn) and (η1, . . . , ηn) in Rn+ such that (θ1, . . . , θn) ⪯w (η1, . . . , ηn), ΣηiXi ≤st ΣθiXi.
compared: linear combinations under weak supermajorization of weights

hypotheses.formal: weak supermajorization: partial sums of smallest of θ >= η's

ambiguity: Weak-supermajorization extension of Theorem 1; note θ ≼w η here means θ 'more equal' in the sense that smallest partial sums of θ are larger (Definition 1(i)).

quote: Theorem 2. If F ∈ H∗, then F satisfies (SD*).
model: linear combination of iid risks vs concentrated position
family: inverted subadditive class H*: F(1/x1) + F(1/x2) >= F(1/(x1+x2)); larger than H, contains super-Pareto distributions

hypotheses.text: (SD*): (Σθi) X1 ≤st ΣθiXi for all θ ∈ Rn+

ambiguity: Also established in Arab et al. (2025, Theorem 3.1); noted as implied by the proof of Theorem 1 here.

quote: Theorem 3. Let F be a continuous distribution function with ess-inf F = 0. Then CP(λ, F) satisfies (SD) for all λ ∈ R++ if and only if F ∈ H.
model: linear combination of iid compound Poisson sums
family: compound Poisson CP(λ, F): X = Σ_{j=1}^N Yj, N ~ Poisson(λ), Yj iid ~ F
compared: weighted sums of iid CP(λ, F) variables under weight majorization (iff characterization)

conclusion.direction: CP(λ, F) satisfies (SD) for all λ > 0 iff F inverted concave: ΣηiXi <=st ΣθiXi for θ ≼ η

quote: Remark 5. By Theorem 3, if F ∈ H, CP(λ, F) satisfies (SD) for any λ ∈ R++. As usual stochastic order is preserved under mixtures (see, e.g., Shaked and Shanthikumar, 2007, Theorem 1.A.3 (d)), if F ∈ H, (SD) holds for the compound mixed Poisson distribution CP(Λ, F) where Λ is a random variable.
model: linear combination of iid compound mixed Poisson sums
family: compound mixed Poisson CP(Λ, F) with random intensity Λ

conclusion.direction: CP(Λ, F) satisfies (SD): ΣηiXi <=st ΣθiXi for θ ≼ η

ambiguity: Stated as a remark (no separate proof) via preservation of st under mixtures.

quote: Theorem 4. Let F be a continuous distribution function with ess-inf F = 0. Then CP(λ, F) satisfies (SD*) for all λ ∈ R++ if and only if F ∈ H∗.
model: linear combination of iid compound Poisson sums vs concentrated position
compared: (Σθi)X1 vs ΣθiXi for CP summands (iff characterization)

conclusion.direction: CP(λ, F) satisfies (SD*) for all λ > 0 iff F inverted subadditive

quote: Theorem 5. The stable distribution Sα(1, β, 0) satisfies (SD) if and only if one of the following conditions holds. (i) α = 1 and β ∈ R+; (ii) α < 1 and β = 1.
model: linear combination of iid stable risks
compared: weighted sums of iid stable variables under weight majorization (iff characterization of (SD))

hypotheses.text: α = 1 and β ∈ R+, or α < 1 and β = 1

conclusion.direction: Sα(1, β, 0) satisfies (SD) iff the stated parameter conditions hold

ambiguity: Part (ii) coincides with the one-sided positive stable case; Theorem 5(ii) noted as equivalent to Theorem 1.2.4 of Ibragimov (2005).

quote: We use the stochastic representation of stable random variables in Weron (1996) to simulate 10000 random samples of two independent stable random variables X1, X2 ∼ Sα(1, β, 0); ... Let Y1 = a1|X1| + a2|X2| and Y2 = b1|X1| + b2|X2|. We consider three cases of the weight vector (a1, a2, b1, b2) = (1, 4, 2, 3), (2, 6, 3, 5) or (3, 8, 5, 6). Figure 1 plots the empirical distribution functions of Y1 and Y2 with α = 0.10 and β = 0 or −0.40, respectively. Figure 2 ... α = 0.90 and β = 0 or 0.30. ... we find that the empirical distributions F̂1 and F̂2 of Y1 and Y2 seem to satisfy F̂1(x) ≥ F̂2(x) for all x.
model: linear combination of absolute values of iid stable variables
compared: Y1 (weights (1,4)/(2,6)/(3,8)) vs Y2 (weights (2,3)/(3,5)/(5,6)) — each b-vector is majorized by the matching a-vector (b ≼ a: b more equal), so (SD) predicts Y1 <=st Y2, i.e. F̂1 >= F̂2 as observed

conclusion.direction: empirical cdfs satisfy F̂1(x) >= F̂2(x) for all x, i.e. Y1 <=st Y2 — supporting the conjecture that absolute stable variables with α <= 1 satisfy (SD)

ambiguity: Simulation-based evidence only (a conjecture, not a theorem); weight pairs are nested majorization-wise: (2,3),(3,5),(5,6) are progressively more dispersed than (1,4),(2,6),(3,8).
